newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Markets fret over Union Pacific bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Markets fret over Union Pacific bid.

text.p: Stock and debt markets reacted with skepticism to Union Pacific Resources Group Inc's hostile offer to buy Pennzoil Co at a 41 percent premium to the target's Friday closing share price.

After Union Pacific announced its proposed deal on Monday its stock fell 7/8 and closed off one at 25-3/8 for the day. Standard & Poor's placed the company's "A" credit rating on CreditWatch with negative implications.

Union Pacific believes that its superior record in turning reserves into actual production and the finance available to accomplish this will enable it to add nine cents a share in annual cash flow when the acquisition is completed.
Analysts, however, worry that Union Pacific may be paying a high premium at a time when energy prices may trend down making it difficult for them to recoup costs.
"This is an acquisition that could look pretty stupid if energy prices fall," said Lysle Brinker, analyst at James Herold.
There are also concerns about the quality of Pennzoil's reserves, said another analyst, who declined to be named.

Union Pacific, currently ranked 14th in terms of natural gas reserves in the U.S. with 2,378 billion cubic feet and Pennzoil ranked 22nd with 1,187 billion will form a combination which places the group in 10th place, ahead of British Petroleum Co Plc and Enron Oil & Gas, but lagging 9th ranked Texaco Inc.

The company said it will raise $2.0 billion in debt to finance 50.1 percent of the $6.4 billion deal, which includes the assumption of $2.2 billion in Pennzoil debt, then pay for the remainder of Pennzoil using its own stock, based on a Union Pacific share price ranging from $25-$30.
Union Pacific believes that its low debt to market capitalisation ratio of 30 percent will permit it to maintain its "A" credit rating, but S&P was less optimistic in its statement.

"Given over $2 billion of incremental debt associated with this transaction, plus the $2.2 billion of Pennzoil debt that would be assumed by UPR, UPR's debt leverage could well increase significantly in the absence of offsetting actions," the rating agency said.
Analysts also note that at a time when most oil and gas companies are looking overseas to create value, Union Pacific is basing its hopes almost entirely on domestic output.
